## By the end of today

::: {.callout-important}

You should be able to:

1. use one reactive expression to keep several outputs consistent;
2. explain what changes when an app moves from your computer to someone else's; and
3. choose between an R package and a hosted web app for a particular audience.

:::

# One calculation, several outputs {.center background-color="#006DAE"}

## A small app with one question

> For a selected WPL season and run threshold, which leading batters remain,
> and how did they score?

The app will show:

* how many batters meet the conditions;
* the leading run-scorer;
* a plot of batting patterns; and
* a small table.

All four claims should describe the **same selection**.

## Demo 1: start with repeated calculations {.scrollable .smaller}

```r
library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

batters <- read.csv("data/wpl_batters.csv")

ui <- page_sidebar(
  title = "WPL batting explorer",
  sidebar = sidebar(
    selectInput(
      "season", "Choose a season",
      choices = sort(unique(batters$season))
    ),
    sliderInput(
      "minimum_runs", "Minimum runs",
      min = 0,
      max = max(batters$runs),
      value = 150,
      step = 25
    )
  ),
  layout_columns(
    value_box(
      title = "Batters shown",
      value = textOutput("number_shown")
    ),
    value_box(
      title = "Leading run-scorer",
      value = textOutput("leading_batter")
    )
  ),
  plotOutput("batters_plot"),
  tableOutput("batters_table")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$number_shown <- renderText({
    batters |>
      filter(
        season == input$season,
        runs >= input$minimum_runs
      ) |>
      nrow()
  })

  output$leading_batter <- renderText({
    filtered <- batters |>
      filter(
        season == input$season,
        runs >= input$minimum_runs
      )

    req(nrow(filtered) > 0)
    filtered$striker[which.max(filtered$runs)]
  })

  output$batters_plot <- renderPlot({
    batters |>
      filter(
        season == input$season,
        runs >= input$minimum_runs
      ) |>
      ggplot(aes(
        x = dot_percent,
        y = boundary_percent,
        size = balls_faced
      )) +
      geom_point(colour = "#006DAE", alpha = 0.7) +
      labs(
        x = "Dot-ball percentage",
        y = "Boundary percentage",
        size = "Balls faced"
      ) +
      theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
  })

  output$batters_table <- renderTable({
    batters |>
      filter(
        season == input$season,
        runs > input$minimum_runs
      ) |>
      arrange(desc(runs)) |>
      select(striker, batting_team, runs, balls_faced) |>
      head(5)
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```

## Duplication creates several sources of truth

```r
# Number and plot
runs >= input$minimum_runs

# Table
runs > input$minimum_runs
```

At an exact threshold, the app disagrees with itself.

## Let the running app draw its dependencies

Start a fresh R session, then enable the reactive log before running the app:

```r
library(reactlog)
reactlog_enable()

shiny::runApp("inst/app")
```

Change each input once, then open the visualiser:

* macOS: **Cmd + F3**
* Windows/Linux: **Ctrl + F3**

The full log may also contain browser and layout nodes. Filter or double-click a
named output to isolate the part of the graph we are discussing.

## Before refactoring: inputs feed every output

```text
input$season -------+---> number
                    +---> leader
input$minimum_runs -+---> plot
                    +---> table
```

## Name the shared calculation

```r
selected_batters <- reactive({
  batters |>
    filter(
      season == input$season,
      runs >= input$minimum_runs
    )
}, label = "selected_batters")
```

* `reactive()` records the calculation and its reactive dependencies.
* `label = "selected_batters"` supplies a readable node name for `reactlog`.
* Calling `selected_batters()` retrieves its current value.

## Call a reactive expression with parentheses

::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Definition

```r
selected_batters <- reactive({
  # calculation
})
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### Use

```r
selected_batters()
```
:::
:::

Without `()`, you have the reactive object—not the data it currently returns.

## Several outputs can consume the same value

```r
output$number_shown <- renderText({
  nrow(selected_batters())
})

output$leading_batter <- renderText({
  selected <- selected_batters()
  selected$striker[which.max(selected$runs)]
})

output$batters_table <- renderTable({
  selected_batters() |>
    arrange(desc(runs)) |>
    select(striker, batting_team, runs)
})
```

## Demo 2: replace `server()` with this version {.scrollable .smaller}

```r
server <- function(input, output, session) {
  selected_batters <- reactive({
    batters |>
      filter(
        season == input$season,
        runs >= input$minimum_runs
      )
  }, label = "selected_batters")

  output$number_shown <- renderText({
    nrow(selected_batters())
  })

  output$leading_batter <- renderText({
    selected <- selected_batters()
    req(nrow(selected) > 0)
    selected$striker[which.max(selected$runs)]
  })

  output$batters_plot <- renderPlot({
    selected_batters() |>
      ggplot(aes(
        x = dot_percent,
        y = boundary_percent,
        size = balls_faced
      )) +
      geom_point(colour = "#006DAE", alpha = 0.7) +
      labs(
        x = "Dot-ball percentage",
        y = "Boundary percentage",
        size = "Balls faced"
      ) +
      theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
  })

  output$batters_table <- renderTable({
    selected_batters() |>
      arrange(desc(runs)) |>
      select(striker, batting_team, runs, balls_faced) |>
      head(5)
  })
}
```

## The dependency graph is the explanation

```text
input$season -------+
                    +---> selected_batters() --+---> number
input$minimum_runs -+                           +---> leader
                                                +---> plot
                                                +---> table
```

Shiny records a dependency whenever reactive code reads an input or another
reactive value.

## Reopen `reactlog` after refactoring

Stop the app, clear the old history and run the revised version:

```r
shiny::reactlogReset()
shiny::runApp("inst/app")
```

Change one input and reopen `reactlog`.

. . .

The graph should now contain one labelled `selected_batters` node between the
two inputs and all four outputs.

## Read the animation from left to right

When `input$minimum_runs` changes, step through the reactive history:

1. the input changes;
2. `selected_batters` becomes invalid;
3. its dependent outputs become invalid;
4. the shared reactive recalculates when needed; and
5. the outputs consume its new value.

## Predict before running

The user changes `input$minimum_runs`.

. . .

1. `selected_batters()` is invalidated.
2. Each output that called it is invalidated.
3. When an output is needed, the shared calculation runs again.
4. All outputs receive the same selected rows.

## Why share a reactive?

Use a shared reactive when several consumers need the same value.

::: {.incremental}

* **Consistency:** outputs cannot quietly apply different rules.
* **Legibility:** the calculation receives a meaningful name.
* **Maintenance:** one rule changes in one place.
* **Efficiency:** Shiny can reuse the current result until a dependency changes.

:::

## Do not make everything reactive

```r
# Loaded once when the R process starts
batters <- read.csv("data/wpl_batters.csv")

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  # Different for each user session
  selected_batters <- reactive({
    batters |>
      filter(season == input$season)
  })
}
```

* Code outside `server()` runs once for the R process and is shared across sessions.
* Code inside `server()` is created separately for each user session.

## A function and a reactive solve different problems

::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Function

```r
select_batters <- function(data,
                           season_value,
                           minimum_runs) {
  data |>
    filter(
      season == season_value,
      runs >= minimum_runs
    )
}
```

Explicit inputs; easy to test outside Shiny.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### Reactive expression

```r
selected_batters <- reactive({
  select_batters(
    batters,
    input$season,
    input$minimum_runs
  )
})
```

Connects the function to the current session.
:::
:::

## Empty data are still a possible value

```r
output$leading_batter <- renderText({
  selected <- selected_batters()

  if (nrow(selected) == 0) {
    return("No batter meets this threshold")
  }

  selected$striker[which.max(selected$runs)]
})
```

## Checkpoint

Which object should own the filter?

1. Each output, so it is self-contained
2. The UI, because the inputs live there
3. One reactive expression used by every relevant output
4. A global variable that is overwritten whenever an input changes

. . .

**3.** It represents the current selection without duplicating the rule or
mixing sessions.

# From your computer to someone else {.center background-color="#006DAE"}

## “Share the app” is incomplete

Who is the audience?

What software do they have?

Who will run R?

Who controls access?

Who maintains the dependencies and data connections?

## Two useful delivery routes

| | R package | Hosted web app |
|---|---|---|
| Primary audience | R users | Browser users |
| R process runs on | User's computer | Hosting server |
| User receives | Installable software | A URL |
| User can reuse functions | Yes | Only through the interface |
| Author maintains | Package releases | A running service |

## A package puts the app beside reusable code

```text
wplcommunicate/
├── DESCRIPTION
├── R/
│   ├── select_batters.R
│   └── run_app.R
└── inst/
    └── app/
        ├── app.R
        └── data/
            └── wpl_batters.csv
```

## `inst/` ships non-R files with the package

During installation, files under `inst/` are copied into the installed package.

```r
run_app <- function() {
  app_dir <- system.file(
    "app",
    package = "wplcommunicate"
  )

  shiny::runApp(app_dir)
}
```

`system.file()` finds the app after installation, wherever the package lives.

## A hosted app moves the R process

::: {.center .f2}

**Local package**<br>
browser ↔ R on the user's computer

<br>

**Hosted app**<br>
user's browser ↔ network ↔ R on a server

:::

## What deployment sends

```r
rsconnect::deployApp(appDir = "inst/app")
```

For a typical hosted deployment, the service needs:

* the app files;
* the R version and package dependencies;
* data or connections required at runtime; and
* configuration that is safe for the server environment.

Only files included in the deployment bundle are available to the server.

## The clean-computer test

Imagine the hosting server has never seen your project.

Can it answer each question?

::: {.incremental}

* Where is every required file?
* Which packages and versions are needed?
* Does filename case match exactly?
* Where do credentials come from?
* Where should durable data be stored?
* What happens when the app restarts?

:::

## Use relative paths within the app bundle

::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Fragile

```r
read.csv(
  "/Users/michael/Desktop/wpl.csv"
)
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### Portable

```r
read.csv("data/wpl_batters.csv")
```
:::
:::

## Declare packages; do not install them in the app

```r
library(shiny)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

or use qualified calls:

```r
dplyr::filter(...)
```

. . .

Do not put this inside `app.R`:

```r
install.packages("dplyr")
```

During deployment, `rsconnect` detects dependencies from calls such as
`library(dplyr)` and `dplyr::filter()`; the hosting service installs them in the
application environment.

## Current hosting choices answer different needs {.smaller}

| Route | Useful when |
|---|---|
| `shinyapps.io` | You want managed Shiny hosting with a straightforward `rsconnect` workflow |
| Posit Connect Cloud | You want GitHub-connected cloud publishing for public data products |
| Posit Connect | An organisation needs authentication, access control and managed publishing |
| Shiny Server | An organisation will operate its own open-source Linux server |

## Choose the route from the constraint

::: {.incremental}

1. **The audience has no R installation.** Host the app.
2. **Analysts need to call the calculation in their own scripts.** Package it.
3. **The app uses confidential organisational data.** Choose hosting with the required identity and access controls.
4. **A colleague needs to inspect and extend the code.** Share the source repository; a URL alone is insufficient.

:::

## Week 11 lesson

::: {.callout-important}
## Summary

* A shared reactive gives several outputs one current source of truth.
* Ordinary functions own reusable calculations; reactives connect them to a user session.
* A package asks the user to run R; a hosted app asks a server to run R.
* Distribution succeeds when files, dependencies, secrets, storage and access work away from the author's computer.
:::
